## Part 1<br>Medicine and computers: from computer-aided diagnosis to AI {.section-slide background-color="#165CAA"}

## Medical tasks that call for computer assistance

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[Diagnosis]{.card-title}

Differential diagnosis, probabilistic reasoning [@ledley1959; @dedombal1972]
:::
::: {.card}
[Medical imaging]{.card-title}

Detection and classification in radiology, retina, skin [@doi2007; @gulshan2016]
:::
::: {.card}
[Decision support]{.card-title}

Alerts, order checking, guideline reminders [@bates1998; @kawamoto2005]
:::
::: {.card}
[Prediction]{.card-title}

Risk scores and early warning, e.g. sepsis [@wong2021]
:::
::: {.card .c-red}
[Documentation]{.card-title}

Records, notes, discharge summaries: a major source of clinician burden
:::
::: {.card .c-red}
[Evidence synthesis]{.card-title}

Searching, screening and extracting data from studies [@gartlehner2024]
:::
::: {.card .c-purple}
[Discovery]{.card-title}

Protein structure, drug targets [@jumper2021]
:::
::: {.card .c-purple}
[Research & education]{.card-title}

Statistical analysis, teaching, assessment
:::
:::

::: {.small .muted .center}
Common thread: **large volume**, **complex reasoning**, **repetitive work**, where humans tire and err.
:::

::: notes
~1.5 min. These are the recurring "pain points". The red cards (documentation, evidence synthesis) are mostly text: that is where LLMs will come in later.
Protein discovery -- alphafold <- alphago
:::

## From computer-aided diagnosis to AI: a timeline

```{r timeline-cad}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| out-width: "100%"
tl = data.frame(
  year = c(1959, 1972, 1976, 1982, 1998, 2005, 2016, 2018, 2020, 2021),
  lab = c("Ledley & Lusted:\nreasoning\nfoundations",
          "de Dombal:\nacute abdominal\npain diagnosis",
          "MYCIN:\nrule-based\nexpert system",
          "INTERNIST-1:\ndiagnostic\nconsultant",
          "Order entry cuts\nmedication errors;\nmammography CAD",
          "Decision support\nworks in 68%\nof trials",
          "Deep learning:\ndiabetic\nretinopathy",
          "First FDA-\nauthorised\nautonomous AI",
          "COVID-19 AI boom;\nbreast cancer\nscreening AI",
          "AlphaFold:\nprotein structure"),
  era = factor(c(rep("Rules & probability", 4), rep("Digitisation & decision support", 2),
          rep("Deep learning", 4)),
    levels = c("Rules & probability", "Digitisation & decision support", "Deep learning"))
)
tl$side = rep(c(1, -1), length.out = nrow(tl))
tl$pos = seq_len(nrow(tl))
ggplot(tl, aes(pos, 0)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = pos, y = 0, yend = side * 0.55, colour = era), linewidth = 1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = era), size = 5) +
  geom_label(aes(y = side * 0.95, label = lab, colour = era), size = 4.9,
             lineheight = 0.9, label.size = 0.7, fill = "white", show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Rules & probability" = theme_red,
                                 "Digitisation & decision support" = theme_purple,
                                 "Deep learning" = theme_blue), name = NULL) +
  geom_text(aes(y = -side * 0.22, label = year), size = 5.5, fontface = "bold", colour = "#272822") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1.25, 1.25)) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(add = 0.8)) +
  theme_void(base_size = 18) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 6)))
```

::: {.tiny .muted}
@ledley1959; @dedombal1972; @shortliffe1976; @miller1982; @bates1998; @doi2007; @kawamoto2005; @gulshan2016; @abramoff2018; @mckinney2020; @wynants2020; @jumper2021
:::

::: notes
~1 min. Three eras. Emphasise that "computer-aided diagnosis" is more than 60 years old: AI in medicine did not start with ChatGPT.
:::

## Era 1: rules and probabilities (1959–1980s)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **@ledley1959**: diagnosis as symbolic logic + probability (Bayes) + value theory
- **@dedombal1972**: prospective real-time comparison in 304 patients with acute abdominal pain
  - Computer accuracy **91.8%** _vs_ most senior clinician **79.6%**
- **MYCIN** [@shortliffe1976]: if–then rules for infections and antibiotic choice
- **INTERNIST-1** [@miller1982]: diagnostic consultant for general internal medicine
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.big-quote}
Bayes' theorem was the first "AI" at the bedside
:::
::: {.small .muted .center}
Knowledge was **hand-coded** by experts (expert system): powerful but brittle and hard to maintain
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
~1.5 min. Point to statisticians in the room: probability and Bayes were at the core of the very first CAD. Expert systems failed to scale because knowledge had to be hand-coded and maintained.
:::

## Era 2: digitisation and decision support (1990s–2000s)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
#### Clinical decision support
- Computerised physician order entry: nonintercepted serious medication errors **↓ 55%** [@bates1998]
- Systematic review of 70 RCTs: decision support improved practice in **68%** of trials; best when **automatic and within workflow** [@kawamoto2005]
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
#### CAD in imaging
- Mammography CAD approved by FDA in 1998 [@doi2007]
- But in real-world use, sensitivity **↑** (not sig.), specificity **↓**, and biopsy rate **↑ 19.7%**; increased potential harms of screening mammography with uncertain clinical benefit [@fenton2007]
:::
::::

::: {.big-quote}
Lesson: **workflow fit** and **real-world evaluation** decide success
:::

::: notes
~1.5 min. Two lessons we will meet again with LLMs: (1) tools succeed when they fit into the workflow; (2) promising lab performance does not guarantee real-world benefit (Fenton 2007). CAD: image enhancement and hand-crafted features with simple classifiers. Not yet DL.
:::

## Era 3: deep learning (2012–today)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Retina**: diabetic retinopathy, AUC 0.99 [@gulshan2016]
- **Skin**: CNN on par with 21 dermatologists [@esteva2017]
- **First autonomous AI** authorised by FDA for diabetic retinopathy: sensitivity 87.2%, specificity 90.7% [@abramoff2018]
- **Breast screening**: fewer false positives and negatives than radiologists [@mckinney2020]
- **COVID-19**: chest CT + clinical data, AUC 0.92 [@mei2020]
- **AlphaFold**: protein structure prediction [@jumper2021]
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-warning}
## A cautionary tale
A widely implemented proprietary sepsis model: AUC **0.63** on external validation, missed **67%** of sepsis cases, but alerts for 18% of all inpatients  -- alert fatigue [@wong2021]
:::
::: {.small .muted}
Reviews: @topol2019; @rajpurkar2022
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
~2 min. Deep learning moved CAD from hand-coded rules to learning from data, mainly images. The Epic sepsis model reminds us: external validation, calibration and alert fatigue are statistical questions. This is where biostatisticians (and R) matter.
:::

## 2020: the COVID-19 AI boom … and its lessons

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
#### The promise
- Urgent need: RT-PCR took up to 2 days and test kits were short [@mei2020]
- AI on chest CT and X-ray looked like a fast answer
- Within months: **hundreds** of diagnostic and prognostic models
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
#### The reality
- Systematic review of 731 prediction models: "Most published prediction model studies were poorly reported and at high risk of bias such that their reported predictive performances are probably optimistic" [@wynants2020]
- Systematic review of 62 studies on machine learning for COVID-19 imaging: **none** "... are of potential clinical use due to methodological flaws and/or underlying biases" [@roberts2021]
:::
::::

::: {.big-quote}
Speed without **methodology** gives models that cannot be used
:::

::: notes
~1.5 min. COVID-19 was the biggest "AI boom" in medicine before ChatGPT. Common problems: poor-quality and biased data, small samples, no external validation, poor reporting (TRIPOD, PROBAST). The same risks apply to the current LLM boom. Wynants et al. figures are from update 3 of the living review.
:::

## Lessons from 60 years of computers in medicine

1. Computers are **assistants**: they extend, not replace, clinicians
2. **Workflow** integration matters as much as accuracy
3. **Evaluation** in real-world settings is non-negotiable: sensitivity, specificity, calibration, impact
4. Most of the remaining burden is **text**: notes, letters, reports, papers

. . .

::: {.big-quote}
… and _text_ is exactly what _large language models_ are good at
:::

::: notes
~1 min. Bridge to Part 2.
:::

## Part 2<br>The rise of large language models {.section-slide background-color="#165CAA"}

::: {.tiny .muted}
@vaswani2017; @radford2018; @devlin2019; @radford2019; @brown2020; @ouyang2022; @openai2022; @openai2023; @touvron2023; @singhal2023; @singhal2025; @guo2025; @sellergren2025; @medgemma15; @mcduff2025; @osullivan2026
:::

::: notes
~2 min. Keep it brief. Key turning points: Transformer (2017), decoder-only generative pre-training (GPT, 2018), scale (GPT-3, 2020), instruction following (InstructGPT) and ChatGPT (Nov 2022). Since then: open-weight models (Llama, Qwen, Gemma...), reasoning models, multimodal, agents. MedGemma (Google, 2025): open-weight medical models built on Gemma 3 (4B multimodal, 27B), updated as MedGemma 1.5 4B in 2026; available in Ollama, so usable from R locally (Part 3).
:::

## Early signals: LLMs know (a lot of) medicine

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
#### Medical exams
- ChatGPT at or near the **passing threshold** on all three USMLE steps, without specialised training [@kung2023]
- Med-PaLM: **67.6%** on MedQA [@singhal2023] → Med-PaLM 2: **86.5%** [@singhal2025]
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
#### Communication with patients
- 195 patient questions from a public forum: evaluators preferred chatbot responses to physician responses in **78.6%** evaluations -- better quality, more empathic than human physicians [@ayers2023]
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note}
## But ...
Of 519 LLM evaluation studies (2022–2024), only **5%** used real patient-care data [@bedi2025]. So, is it valid?
:::

::: notes
~1.5 min. US Medical Licensing Exam (USMLE), MedQA: US Medical Licensing Exam-style questions.
:::

## How medicine benefits from LLMs: by task

| Task | Example study | Key finding |
|:-----|:--------------|:------------|
| **Diagnosis** | AMIE, 302 differential diagnoses of complex cases [@mcduff2025] | Top-10 accuracy: AMIE alone 59.1% _vs_ unassisted clinicians 33.6% |
| | Physician RCT [@goh2024] | LLM access did _not_ improve physicians' diagnostic reasoning; but the LLM alone scored 16 percentage points higher than physicians with conventional resources |
| | Cardiology RCT [@osullivan2026] | Fewer clinical errors with AMIE assistance (13.1% _vs_ 24.3%) |
| **Documentation** | Ambient AI scribes, RCTs [@lukac2025; @afshar2025] | Less time in notes, less work exhaustion; occasional inaccuracies |
| **Summarisation** | 4 clinical summarisation tasks [@vanveen2024] | LLM summaries were superior to medical experts' in 36% of cases (equivalent in 45%) |
| **Information extraction** | 1026 lung cancer, 191 pediatric osteosarcoma pathology reports [@huang2024] | classification accuracy: 89% and 98.6% respectively |
| **Evidence synthesis** | Data extraction from RCTs for systematic review [@gartlehner2024] | 96.3% accuracy over 160 data elements from 10 papers |
| **Dialogue / history-taking** | Conversational AMIE [@tu2025] | Higher diagnostic accuracy than primary care physicians in text-based consultations |

::: notes
~3 min. Pick 2–3 rows to highlight. AMIE (Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer).
:::

## Human + AI collaboration

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- RCT of 70 clinicians: AI as **first** or **second opinion** improved diagnostic accuracy (85% and 82% _vs_ 75% with conventional resources)  -- complementary role of AI [@everett2026]
- Just giving clinicians a chatbot was not enough -- emphasis on AI as assistant [@goh2024]
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.big-quote}
An LLM is an **assistant**, not a replacement
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
~1 min. Echo Part 1 lesson: workflow matters.
:::

## Risks we must manage

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- `r warn` **Hallucination**: fluent but fabricated content [@wang2024; @thirunavukarasu2023]
- `r warn` **Bias**: gender-, race-biased responses [@wang2024; @omiye2023]
- `r warn` **Inconsistency**: different answers to the same question [@omiye2023]
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- `r warn` **Privacy**: patient data sent to cloud providers
- `r warn` **Changing models**: behaviour shifts between versions, opaque training data [@iozzia2026]
- `r warn` **Evaluation gap**: few studies on real patient data [@bedi2025]
:::
::::

::: {.big-quote}
These are **statistical** and **governance** problems, not only engineering ones
:::

::: notes
~1.5 min. Local/small language models (SLMs) are one answer to privacy and versioning (my SLM book review). Evaluation, agreement, bias and reproducibility are bread-and-butter for biostatisticians.
:::

## Part 3<br>Where `r fontawesome::fa('r-project', fill = 'white')` stands {.section-slide background-color="#165CAA"}

## `r py` Python dominates LLM development

- Pre-training, fine-tuning and serving: PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM, …
- In 2024, Python overtook JavaScript as the most used language on GitHub, driven by AI and data science [@octoverse2024]
- Practitioner LLM books assume Python and PyTorch skills, e.g. @iozzia2026

. . .

::: {.big-quote}
So… is `r r_blue` still relevant for LLMs in medicine?
:::

::: notes
~1 min. Be honest: for building and training models, Python wins, and that is fine.
:::

## Most medical users do not _build_ LLMs; they _use_ them

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
#### Build the engine `r py`
- Pre-training from scratch
- Fine-tuning, quantisation
- Serving at scale
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
#### Drive the car `r r_blue`
- **Inference**: prompt a model via API or locally
- **Structure** text into analysable data
- **Evaluate** the outputs statistically
- **Report** and **share**: Quarto, Shiny
:::
::::

::: {.big-quote}
For the second column, `r r_blue` is a first-class citizen
:::

::: notes
~1 min. Analogy from Iozzia's SLM book: the model is the engine; an application needs the rest of the car. R users mostly need the car, not the engine factory.
:::

## Where `r r_blue` stands

::: {.cards .three}
::: {.card}
[1. Inference]{.card-title}

Cloud APIs (OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, …) and **local** models via Ollama: same R session, one interface [@ellmer; @rollama]
:::
::: {.card}
[2. Prototyping research ideas]{.card-title}

Test an idea in minutes, next to your data, your models and your plots
:::
::: {.card}
[3. Text → data]{.card-title}

Extract structured variables from notes and papers straight into data frames [@tidyllm; @arifin2026workshop]
:::
::: {.card .c-red}
[4. Evaluation]{.card-title}

Accuracy, agreement, CIs, trials of LLM tools: biostatistics' home turf [@vitals]
:::
::: {.card .c-red}
[5. Simple apps]{.card-title}

Shiny + chat UI for patient education or data Q&A in a few lines [@shinychat]
:::
::: {.card .c-red}
[6. Reproducible reporting]{.card-title}

Prompts, model versions, seeds and results in one Quarto document
:::
::: {.card .c-purple}
[7. Privacy-first local LLMs]{.card-title}

Patient data stay on your machine with Ollama + R [@arifin2026book]
:::
::: {.card .c-purple}
[8. Trusted in clinical research]{.card-title}

R-based submission packages reviewed by the FDA [@rconsortium2024]
:::
::: {.card .c-purple}
[9. RAG, tools & agents]{.card-title}

Retrieval over guidelines, tool calling, MCP: R functions as tools [@ragnar; @mcptools]
:::
:::

::: notes
~2 min. These are the answers to "in what context?". Points 1–3 were in the abstract; 4–9 are the ones I want to add. If Python is needed (e.g. a Hugging Face model), reticulate bridges the gap. Evidence for no 8: https://github.com/RConsortium/submissions-pilot3-adam
:::

## The `r r_blue` + LLM package landscape

| Purpose | Packages |
|:--------|:---------|
| **Unified chat interface** (cloud + local) | **`ellmer`** [@ellmer], **`tidyllm`** [@tidyllm] |
| **Local models via Ollama** | **`rollama`** [@rollama], `ollamar` [@ollamar] |
| **LLM over data frame columns** | `mall` [@mall] |
| **Retrieval-augmented generation** | `ragnar` [@ragnar], `rchroma` |
| **Evaluation** | `vitals` [@vitals] |
| **Apps** | `shinychat` [@shinychat], `querychat` (natural language → SQL over data) |
| **Coding assistants** | `btw` [@btw], `gander` [@gander], `chores` [@chores], `chattr` [@chattr], `gptstudio` [@gptstudio] |
| **Model Context Protocol** | `mcptools` [@mcptools]: let assistants use your R session, and R use MCP tools |
| **Vision** | `kuzco` (computer vision with LLMs) [@kuzco] |

## Showcase: tasks from Parts 1 & 2, done in `r r_blue`

| # | Medical task (Parts 1 & 2) | Package | What we do |
|:-:|:---------------------------|:--------|:-----------|
| 1 | Patient communication, translation | `rollama` | Explain a finding in simple Malay, locally |
| 2 | Triage / text classification | `rollama` | Zero-shot classification of complaints |
| 3 | Information extraction | `tidyllm` | Structure clinical notes into a data frame |
| 4 | Extraction **+ evaluation** | `ellmer` | Extract labs from many notes, check against gold standard |
| 5 | Decision support (calculation) | `ellmer` | Tool calling: R computes eGFR, the LLM explains |
| 6 | Patient education, grounded in a document | `ragnar` | Retrieval (RAG) over a Malay Wikipedia page |
| 7 | Simple app | `ellmer` + `shinychat` + `ragnar` | Patient-education chatbot that cites the page |

::: {.small .muted}
All examples use open-weight models through Ollama on a local PC, except where noted. Full code and output: demo document (next slides).

## Practical considerations

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
#### Privacy & ethics
- Identifiable patient data → **local models** or approved, contracted services only
- Ethics approval and data governance as for any data processing

#### Reproducibility
- Record **model name + version**, prompts, `seed`, `temperature`
- Keep prompts and code in Quarto / Git
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
#### Validation
- Gold standard on a sample; report accuracy **with CIs**, agreement, errors by type
- Re-validate when the model changes

#### Resources
- Local: gaming-grade GPU for 3–14B models
- Cloud: cost per token, rate limits, downtime
:::
::::

::: notes
~1.5 min. These are the things reviewers and ethics committees will ask.
:::

## Take-home messages

1. Computers have assisted medicine for **60+ years**; LLMs are the newest assistant, and they speak **text**
2. LLMs already help with **diagnosis, documentation, summarisation and extraction**, but **evaluation on real data** lags behind
3. `r py` Python builds the models; `r r_blue` is **highly relevant** for **using** them in medicine: inference, prototyping, text → data, evaluation, apps, reporting
4. Start with **`rollama`** (local), structure data with **`tidyllm`**, grow with **`ellmer`** and **`ragnar`**
5. Our biostatistics strengths, **validation, reproducibility, inference**, are exactly what medical LLM work needs

::: {.big-quote}
Medicine × LLM × `r r_blue`: the centre of the Venn diagram is ours to build `r heart_red`
:::
